raw_text:
Plan intended to elaborate on an example of a 'repeated responses to the same question' research objective hypothesis that you stated in the discussion.


Identify what needs to hold constant and/or what needs to be changed to observe corresponding effects and to test linked explanations. Spell out the null hypothesis you decided is most appropriate for your objective. State alternative hypotheses for rejection and failure to reject the null, as appropriate for the research purpose.

Where possible, review at least 2 suites of parameters. Additional parameters – other parameters on which explanations are readily linked – should be listed.

Research Plan

Plan - what research you will need to do. This is a list of things you will try and then assess what you conclude from it. You can have multiple plans.


Research Plan


The most precise definitions of D/P/B you can think of for your hypotheses. Any other variables that behave differently for the 3 hypotheses? If the definition is a numeric one, make sure you can unambiguously calculate intermediate values such that their differences are very small for the hypothesis situations. Observations/drawings/figures etc might help here. The analysis requires that the measurement precision is well specified, at the least in terms of inflection points before and after small differences.

- If the definition is a description, specify/indicate features that aid observations, existence checks, and maybe explanatory controls; and just note quality.

First, define or sketch all variables needed to instantiate the null hypothesis and discern the differences between it and the other alternatives. For example: Include features being observed, measured, likely durations for which the experiments will run, and their primary and secondary performance correlates.

Second, note whether any of the contextual differences among alternatives need different parameter values, reference classes, or selective inducers for the D/P/B/Porenthods respectively to avoid confound variables.

Third, note whether the alternatives may generate confound or biased observables, and how those would be removed - especially for selectivities.

Fourth, note whether control information will be in and/or out of scope for any selection effects or selective inducer effects.


Generally, any differences among the alternatives' D/P/B parameters?

If yes, what features might distinguish the changes and/or explain them.

How results will be quantified – i.e. analyzing the effects of changing something.

How will the results be determined evident? Are you comparing just one difference set or will it be considered with/against other difference sets?

What is the forcing function or objective of the analysis?

This is just a very brief outline of what you'll be thinking about as we go through it. Don't spend extra time on it; we will be paused for a moment to discuss.


Limitations to the work.
For example, what might not work; what is missing (data, time, options), resources etc.
What the findings and related studies are not suggesting.
(The stopping rules would be part.)


Some ideas:

[aim to get something sensible and analytical working; reliance on the 'best ideas' of library abstracts is also a goal.]
* abstract a data source you have used before, then attempt to expand your use and scope

* link projects from different sources and scope; if you were recording different variables from different research scenarios, combine the info from multiple sites, multiple eras and/or across many different people; take new approaches

* or map multiple data sources into one scoring/billing/voting/rating or alternates - for example bills or commissions or vars (strength?) you posit proportional effects for; etc and relaying back to earlier observations you clump/try to convert to data/input,

* scale them to generate histograms to try to generalise better observations between data sources -----------

* and break them & group them - for example if you were repeating, aggregate, split apart,

* do you go or say use how exemplars or as cover or many different examples to flog hypotheses as to normal to abnormal difference for different/dissimilar costs?

* blue skies - hypothesise moon-landing conspiracy.

* Analogise them to "assume a can opener"

* project - merging in a different basis?


Key Output 2 - Metastructures

The next line also will be one of the less obvious destinations in your dissertation research and refinement – linkages. Research can be meta-analysed in multiple ways.

The project's research plan identifies initial discovery of the data's categories structures by its quantified span, reach and differences. The direct output from the plan's detailed 'planting and harvesting' tests and experiments are usually statistical or probabilistic - a set of non-hypothesis testable quantitative predictions about the future that determine the project's merit.

Not all research plans are valuable in this manner just because the Data/ Measurements / Experiments phases are technically well designed and executed, and the analysis of multiple comments and dissents steps towards acceptable numeric analyses.

But the conclusions themselves require that the final analyses or probabilistic conclusions be seeded by structured, semi-classic research foci, rather than loose or casual exploration. Necessarily, each unique independent clean test adds or subtracts its value to the bundle. Thoroughness augments decisiveness for that determinism.

The generation step for introduction of synthesis or key-linkages is the random character of France in the 1770s version. Though a final selectivity selection samples overall output for connections, the generation is the primary production.
